decks.title: Controlling — Part 1: Meaning, Importance and Limitations
goals: Explain the meaning and features of controlling
Identify the importance of controlling in business situations
Identify the limitations of controlling in a case
Explain why planning and controlling are inseparable

slides.heading: Controlling
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what controlling **is**, its **features**, why it **matters**, its **limits** and its link with **planning**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what controlling is, its features, why it matters, its limits, and how it links with planning
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A cricket captain plans a target score, but during the match he keeps checking the run rate and changes the batting order if needed. Managers do the same. In this chapter we study controlling, the function that checks whether work is going according to plan. Part one covers its meaning, features, importance and limitations, and its close link with planning.

slides.heading: What is controlling?
slides.body_md: **Controlling** makes sure that activities happen **according to plan**, and corrects them where they do not.

headers: At an imagined school canteen in Bhopal

visual.alt: Table showing controlling at an imagined school canteen: the plan was 400 lunches by 1.15 pm, 360 were served, the gap was 40 lunches, and the action is to start cooking rice 20 minutes earlier
visual.caption: Controlling compares what happened with what was planned, then acts.

slides.narration: Look at this imagined school canteen. It planned four hundred lunches by quarter past one. Only three hundred and sixty were ready. The gap is forty lunches. So the manager decides to start cooking rice twenty minutes earlier. That whole cycle of checking results against the plan and fixing the gap is controlling.

slides.heading: Features of controlling

rows: Keeps the organisation moving towards its planned goals
Done at every level and in every kind of organisation
Goes on all the time, not only at the year end
Every manager must control the work under them
Checks past work and improves future work

visual.alt: Table of five features of controlling: goal-oriented, pervasive, continuous, a primary function of every manager, and both backward- and forward-looking

slides.narration: Controlling is goal-oriented: it keeps the organisation moving towards its goals. It is pervasive, found at every level and in every kind of organisation, from a factory to a school. It is continuous, not a once-a-year check. Every manager must perform it. And it looks both backward, at work already done, and forward, at how to do better.

slides.heading: Quick check: which feature?
slides.body_md: A chairperson, a plant manager and a shift supervisor each review results in their own area. Which feature is this?
slides.narration: Count the levels of management in the question. What does it tell you when every level is doing the same function?

slides.heading: Looking back and looking forward

nodes.label: Better methods and standards next month (look forward)

visual.alt: Flow showing controlling looking back at last month's results, comparing them with standards, finding causes, and improving methods and standards for next month
visual.caption: Back and forward together

slides.narration: Some students think controlling only looks back, like a post-mortem. Not true. Yes, it measures work already done. But the reason we measure is to find causes and improve methods and standards for next time. So controlling looks back in order to look forward.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: spotting a feature in a case
slides.body_md: Board cases quote a line and ask for the feature.
bullets: Step 1 — Underline the clue words
Step 2 — Match them to one feature
Step 3 — Name the feature and explain it with the words of the case

rows: "The supervisor checks quality every hour of every shift"
"Even the small village school checks its exam results"
"Last year's delays were studied to plan quicker deliveries"

visual.alt: Table of three case lines with their clue words and features: hourly checks show it is continuous, a village school checking results shows it is pervasive, and studying last year's delays to plan quicker deliveries shows it looks back and forward

slides.narration: Let us practise with three imagined lines. Checking quality every hour of every shift shows that controlling is continuous. A small village school checking its results shows that it is pervasive. Studying last year's delays to plan quicker deliveries shows it looks both back and forward. Always name the feature first, then explain it using the case.

slides.heading: Why control? Six points of importance

rows: Gaps are spotted and closed in time
Shows when a target is too high or too low
People know what is expected and how they will be judged
Departments work to standards that fit together

visual.alt: Table of six points of importance of controlling: accomplishing goals, judging accuracy of standards, efficient use of resources, improving motivation, order and discipline, and facilitating coordination

slides.narration: Why do organisations control? It helps them accomplish goals, because gaps are spotted in time. It shows whether standards are accurate. It makes resources go further by cutting waste. It motivates people, who know what is expected. It keeps order and discipline. And it helps coordination, because every department works to standards that fit together.

slides.heading: Quick check: which importance?
slides.body_md: Daily stock checks at a medicine warehouse stop cases of missing strips. Which importance of controlling is this?
slides.narration: Think about what daily checks do to people who might be tempted to take something.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: finding importance in a case
slides.body_md: Match each line from an imagined bus depot to one point of importance.
bullets: Less waste → efficient use of resources
Dishonesty stops → order and discipline
Clear basis of reward → motivation
Target reviewed → accuracy of standards

headers: Line in a case (imagined bus depot, Mysuru)
rows: "Tyre wear is now checked weekly, and fewer tyres are scrapped early"
"Ticket cash is counted twice a day, and shortages have stopped"
"Drivers know that on-time trips decide their award"
"No route ever met the 98% on-time target, so it was reviewed"

visual.alt: Table linking lines from an imagined bus depot in Mysuru to the importance of controlling: weekly tyre checks show efficient use of resources, twice-daily cash counts show order and discipline, an award for on-time trips shows motivation, and reviewing an unmet target shows judging accuracy of standards

slides.narration: Here is an imagined bus depot in Mysuru. Fewer tyres scrapped early means resources are used efficiently. Cash shortages stopping shows order and discipline. Drivers knowing that on-time trips decide their award shows motivation. And a target that no route ever met being reviewed shows that controlling judges the accuracy of standards.

slides.heading: Limitations of controlling

rows: Morale, courtesy and satisfaction resist numbers
Policy, technology and rivals lie outside the firm
Close checks can feel like distrust
Systems need money, time and effort

visual.alt: Table of four limitations of controlling: hard to set quantitative standards, little control on external factors, resistance from employees, and high cost

slides.narration: Controlling is powerful, but it has four limits. Some standards, like courtesy or morale, are hard to put into numbers. The firm has little control over outside factors such as government policy, new technology or rivals. Employees may resist checks they see as distrust. And control systems cost money, time and effort, which small firms may not afford.

slides.heading: Quick check: a limitation
slides.body_md: A hospital cannot express "courtesy of nurses" in numbers. Which limitation is this?
slides.narration: Ask yourself whether the problem is about measuring, about the outside world, about people objecting, or about money.

slides.heading: Telling the limitations apart
columns:
**Inside the firm**

People object to checks (resistance); the system costs too much (cost); the quality cannot be counted (standards).

**Outside the firm**

A new duty, a flood, a rival's price cut or a new technology (external factors).

rows: Can it be put into numbers?
If not: difficulty in setting quantitative standards
Did it start outside the firm?
If so: little control on external factors
Are people objecting to the checks?
Is the system worth more than it saves?

visual.alt: Table of four questions to identify a limitation: whether it can be put into numbers, whether it started outside the firm, whether people object to checks, and whether the system costs more than it saves

slides.narration: In a case, ask four quick questions. Can the thing be put into numbers? Did the problem start outside the firm? Are people objecting to the checks? Is the system worth what it costs? The answer points you to the right limitation, and you can then quote the line that proves it.

slides.narration: Planning and controlling go together like the two blades of a pair of scissors. Planning sets the goals and standards. Without them, controlling has nothing to measure against, so it is blind. Without controlling, nobody knows whether the plan is working, so planning is meaningless. And the lessons from control flow back into the next plan.

slides.heading: Both look back and forward
slides.body_md: Planning is not only forward-looking, and controlling is not only backward-looking.

rows: Using past results and control reports
Setting goals for the coming period

visual.alt: Table showing that planning looks back by using past results and looks forward by setting goals, and that controlling looks back by measuring work done and forward by correcting causes and revising standards

slides.narration: A common exam question asks whether planning only looks forward and controlling only looks back. The better answer is no. Planning uses past results and control reports to set future goals. Controlling measures past work, but its corrective action and revised standards shape the future. So both functions look back and forward.

slides.heading: Quick check: feedback into the plan
slides.body_md: Control findings show that sales targets for the hills were unrealistic, so next year's plan lowers them. What does this show?
slides.narration: Notice the direction of the arrow here: from control results back into the next plan.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Work goes as planned; gaps are corrected
Goal-oriented, pervasive, continuous, looks back and forward
Goals, standards, resources, motivation, discipline, coordination

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning, features, six points of importance, four limitations and the link with planning

slides.narration: To sum up: controlling makes sure work goes as planned and corrects gaps. It is goal-oriented, pervasive and continuous, and looks back and forward. It helps reach goals, test standards, save resources, motivate people, keep discipline and coordinate departments. It is limited by measurement, outside factors, resistance and cost. And it is inseparable from planning.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: In case questions, **name** the feature, importance or limitation, then **quote** the line.
Do not confuse "judging accuracy of standards" with "accomplishing goals".
External factors start **outside** the firm; resistance comes from **employees**.
"Planning without controlling is meaningless; controlling without planning is blind."
5 marks: five headed points, each with one line of explanation.
slides.narration: Marks in this chapter come from naming the right idea and proving it with the case. Write the name of the feature or importance as a heading, then quote the exact words. Keep similar ideas apart: a target found to be wrong is about accuracy of standards, not about reaching goals. And learn the line about planning and controlling; it often earns a mark.

decks.title: Controlling — Part 2: The Controlling Process
goals: List and explain the five steps of the controlling process in order
Calculate a deviation and express it as a percentage of the standard
Apply critical point control and management by exception to decide what needs attention
Suggest corrective action that removes the cause of a deviation

slides.heading: The controlling process
slides.body_md: Part 2 — five steps: **set**, **measure**, **compare**, **analyse**, **correct**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the five steps of the controlling process, from setting standards to correcting deviations
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In part two we see how managers actually control. There are five steps: setting standards, measuring performance, comparing the two, analysing the deviations, and taking corrective action. We will also learn two useful ideas for analysing deviations, critical point control and management by exception, and practise some simple calculations.

slides.heading: Five steps of controlling

visual.alt: Flow of the five steps of the controlling process: set performance standards, measure actual performance, compare with standards, analyse deviations and take corrective action
visual.caption: The controlling process

slides.narration: Here are the five steps in order. First, set performance standards. Second, measure actual performance. Third, compare actual performance with the standards. Fourth, analyse the deviations to find which matter and why they happened. Fifth, take corrective action. Remember the order: set, measure, compare, analyse, correct.

slides.heading: Step 1: setting performance standards
slides.body_md: Standards are the **criteria** against which actual performance is judged.

rows: Improve the goodwill of the brand

visual.alt: Table contrasting quantitative standards such as 300 bicycles a day, a cost of 200 rupees per jar and 98 in 100 parcels within 48 hours with qualitative standards such as goodwill, morale and making guests feel welcome
visual.caption: Standards should be precise and also flexible enough to revise.

slides.narration: Standards can be quantitative, such as three hundred bicycles a day or two hundred rupees per jar. Others are qualitative, such as goodwill or morale, and have no simple number. Good standards are precise, so that performance can be measured against them, and flexible, so that they can be changed when conditions change.

slides.heading: Quick check: put the steps in order
slides.body_md: Arrange the steps followed at an imagined bicycle factory.
slides.narration: Start with the target, and finish with the repair. What must happen in between?

slides.heading: Step 2: measuring actual performance
slides.body_md: Measure in the **same units** as the standard, objectively and reliably.

rows: A floor manager watches the packing line
Weighing 50 soap cakes from each batch
Weekly sales report from each branch

visual.alt: Table of three measurement techniques: personal observation, sample checking and performance reports, each with an imagined example

slides.narration: The second step is to measure what has actually been done. Managers use personal observation, sample checking, where a few items represent a whole batch, and performance reports from branches or departments. Measurement should be in the same units as the standard, otherwise comparison is impossible.

slides.narration: Now compare. This imagined bicycle factory has a standard of three hundred bicycles a day. Look at each bar against the dashed line. Monday is exactly on target, Wednesday is a little above, and Tuesday, Thursday and Friday are below. Thursday is far below. Comparison tells us whether there is a gap, and how big it is.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: deviation as a percentage
slides.body_md: Deviation = actual minus standard; express it as a percentage of the standard.
bullets: Step 1 — Find the gap: actual − standard
Step 2 — Divide the gap by the standard
Step 3 — Multiply by 100 and say whether it is a shortfall or an excess

visual.alt: Table of an imagined dairy's standards and actuals: milk collected 10,000 against 9,400 litres, 6 per cent short; torn packets 200 against 260, 30 per cent over; vans on time 50 against 48, 4 per cent short
visual.caption: Percentage deviation = deviation ÷ standard × 100.

slides.narration: Here is an imagined dairy in Karnal. It aimed to collect ten thousand litres a day but collected nine thousand four hundred: six hundred litres short, which is six per cent of the standard. Torn packets were sixty above the standard of two hundred, that is thirty per cent. Two vans out of fifty left late, which is four per cent.

slides.heading: Quick check: work out the percentage
slides.body_md: A shoe unit has a standard of 500 pairs a day and produces 460. What is the deviation as a percentage of the standard?
slides.narration: Find the gap first, then divide it by the standard, not by the actual figure.

slides.heading: Step 4: analysing deviations
slides.body_md: Not every gap deserves the manager's time. Ask three questions.

nodes.label: Is it a key result area? (critical point control)
Is it beyond the permissible limit? (management by exception)
What caused it? (machines, people, materials, standards, outside factors)

visual.alt: Flow of analysing deviations: check whether the area is a key result area, whether the deviation is beyond the permissible limit, what caused it, and then decide the corrective action
visual.caption: Three questions before acting

slides.narration: Once we know the gaps, we analyse them. Is the gap in a key result area? Is it bigger than the limit we can live with? And what caused it: machines, people, materials, an unrealistic standard, or something outside the firm? Only after these questions can the manager choose the right action.

slides.heading: Critical point control

rows: Cost of steel in a car-parts firm
Safety readings in a chemical plant

visual.alt: Table contrasting key result areas such as steel cost, safety readings and cash collection with minor areas such as office tea, garden upkeep and notice-board printing
visual.caption: A small slip in a key result area hurts the whole firm.

slides.narration: Critical point control means focusing on key result areas, the ones that affect the whole organisation. In a car parts firm, even a small rise in the cost of steel hurts profit, while a big rise in the tea bill hardly matters. So managers watch steel closely and leave minor areas to their juniors.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning and features
sections.body_md:
**Controlling** is the management function of seeing that actual work conforms to plans, and of correcting deviations when it does not. Every manager, at every level, controls the work under them.

**Features**
1. **Goal-oriented** — it keeps the organisation on course to its goals.
2. **Pervasive** — at all levels, in business and non-business organisations alike.
3. **Continuous** — the cycle of checking never stops.
4. **A primary function** of every manager.
5. **Backward- and forward-looking** — it reviews work done, and its findings improve future work.

sections.heading: 2. Importance of controlling
sections.body_md:
1. **Accomplishing organisational goals** — gaps are found early and closed.
2. **Judging accuracy of standards** — repeated large gaps (above or below) show that a standard needs revision.
3. **Making efficient use of resources** — working to standards reduces waste and spoilage.
4. **Improving employee motivation** — employees know beforehand what is expected and the basis of appraisal.
5. **Ensuring order and discipline** — close checks reduce dishonest behaviour.
6. **Facilitating coordination in action** — each department works to standards that fit with the others.

sections.heading: 3. Limitations of controlling
sections.body_md:
1. **Difficulty in setting quantitative standards** — morale, courtesy and job satisfaction cannot easily be counted, so control over them is less effective.
2. **Little control on external factors** — government policy, technology, competition and natural events lie outside the firm.
3. **Resistance from employees** — strict checks (cameras, tracking) may be seen as a curb on freedom.
4. **Costly affair** — control systems take money, time and effort; the benefit should exceed the cost, which can be hard for small firms.

sections.heading: 4. Planning and controlling
sections.body_md:
Planning and controlling are **inseparable twins**. Planning sets goals and standards; controlling checks whether they are being achieved.

- Planning **without** controlling is **meaningless**: no one knows whether the plan works.
- Controlling **without** planning is **blind**: there is nothing to measure against.

**Both look back and forward.** Planning draws on past results and control reports to set future goals; controlling reviews completed work, but corrective action and revised standards improve the future.

sections.body_md:
**1. Setting performance standards** — quantitative (units, cost, time, defects) or qualitative (goodwill, morale). Standards should be **precise** and **flexible**.

**3. Comparing actual performance with standards** — reveals whether there is a deviation and how large it is.

**Percentage deviation** = (actual − standard) ÷ standard × 100, stated as a shortfall or an excess.

sections.heading: 6. Steps 4 and 5: analysing deviations and corrective action
sections.body_md:
**4. Analysing deviations**
- **Critical point control:** focus on **key result areas** (KRAs) that affect the entire organisation, e.g. raw-material cost or safety, rather than on everything equally.
- **Management by exception:** only **significant deviations beyond a permissible limit** are brought to senior managers; minor ones are handled lower down. If managers try to control everything, they may end up controlling nothing.
- Then find the **cause**: machines, people, materials, unrealistic standards or outside factors.

**5. Taking corrective action** — remove the cause (repair, train, reorder, motivate), or **revise the standard** if it was unrealistic. No action is needed when the deviation is within the limit.

questions.stem_md: Controlling, as a function of management, means

options.text_md: deciding in advance what is to be done and how
ensuring that activities in the organisation are performed as per the plans
filling and keeping filled the positions in the organisation structure
guiding and motivating subordinates towards goals

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ensuring that activities in the organisation are performed as per the plans. Controlling checks that work actually happens according to plan and corrects deviations. Deciding in advance is planning, filling positions is staffing, and guiding and motivating is directing.

questions.stem_md: Controlling is called a **goal-oriented** function because it

options.text_md: is performed only by top management
is performed only once, at the end of the year
replaces the need for planning
makes sure that resources are used to achieve the predetermined goals

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** makes sure that resources are used to achieve the predetermined goals. Its whole purpose is to see that the organisation reaches the goals set in plans. It is done at every level, continuously, and it depends on planning rather than replacing it.

questions.stem_md: At Sitara Textiles (imagined), the chairperson reviews yearly profit, the plant manager reviews monthly output and a shift supervisor checks daily attendance. This shows that controlling is

options.text_md: pervasive
a backward-looking function only
the primary function of management
needed only in large firms

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** pervasive. Managers at all three levels perform controlling, each for their own area, so it is pervasive. Controlling also looks forward, planning (not controlling) is the primary function, and small firms need control too.

questions.stem_md: Why is controlling described as both a **backward-looking** and a **forward-looking** function?

options.text_md: It looks only at past records and never affects future work
It is performed before planning and again after directing
It checks performance that has already taken place and also uses the findings to improve future performance
It deals with past employees and future recruits

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It checks performance that has already taken place and also uses the findings to improve future performance. Measuring what was done is backward-looking; the corrective action and better standards it leads to are forward-looking. It does not ignore the future, it does not come before planning, and it is not about recruitment.

questions.stem_md: For three months running, every salesperson at Vayu Coolers (imagined) beats the target by more than 40 per cent, even in a weak season. Management raises the targets. Which importance of controlling does this show?

options.text_md: Ensuring order and discipline
Improving employee motivation
Judging the accuracy of standards
Facilitating coordination in action

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Judging the accuracy of standards. Results far above the standard in a weak season suggest the standard was set too low; controlling reveals this and the standard is revised. Order and discipline, motivation and coordination are other benefits, but none of them is about revising targets.

questions.stem_md: After daily stock checks began at a medicine warehouse in Lucknow (imagined), cases of missing strips stopped. Which importance of controlling is reflected?

options.text_md: Ensuring order and discipline
Judging the accuracy of standards
Facilitating coordination in action
Accomplishing organisational goals

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Ensuring order and discipline. Close checks reduce dishonest behaviour and create discipline among employees. The other options are real benefits of controlling, but the case is about checking misconduct.

questions.stem_md: How does a good control system improve **employee motivation**?

options.text_md: Employees are punished for every small mistake
Employees no longer need any supervision
Employees are allowed to set their own standards without review
Employees know in advance what is expected and on what basis their performance will be appraised

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Employees know in advance what is expected and on what basis their performance will be appraised. Clear standards and a fair basis of appraisal motivate people to perform. Punishing every slip demotivates, supervision still exists, and standards are set by management and reviewed.

questions.stem_md: Controlling **facilitates coordination** because

options.text_md: it removes the need for departments to communicate
each department works to predetermined standards that are well balanced with those of other departments
it is carried out only by the coordination department
it lets each department fix its own goals freely

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** each department works to predetermined standards that are well balanced with those of other departments. When every department has standards fitted to the others and is checked against them, their efforts move together. Communication is still needed, there is no separate coordination department, and free goal-setting would break coordination.

questions.stem_md: Sahyog Hospital (imagined) wants to control the "courtesy of nurses towards patients" but cannot express it in numbers. Which limitation of controlling is this?

options.text_md: Difficulty in setting quantitative standards
Little control on external factors
Resistance from employees
Costly affair

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Difficulty in setting quantitative standards. Courtesy is a behaviour that is hard to measure, so performance cannot be compared against a numeric standard. The case has nothing to do with outside factors, employee opposition or cost.

questions.stem_md: A sudden change in import duty raised the cost of steel for Lakshmi Fabricators (imagined), and nothing in its control system could prevent it. This shows that

options.text_md: controlling is a costly affair
an organisation has little control on external factors
employees resist controls
standards cannot be set in numbers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** an organisation has little control on external factors. Duties, technology, competition and policy are outside the firm; controlling cannot stop them. The case is not about cost, resistance or measurability.

questions.stem_md: Workers at a call centre in Mohali (imagined) protested when cameras were installed to monitor their breaks. Which limitation of controlling is shown?

options.text_md: Costly affair
Little control on external factors
Resistance from employees
Difficulty in setting quantitative standards

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Resistance from employees. Employees often see close monitoring as a restriction on their freedom and oppose it. The protest is about the control itself, not its cost, external factors or measurement.

questions.stem_md: A small bakery in Shillong (imagined) was advised to buy software worth ₹4 lakh to track the weight of every loaf, though its yearly profit is about ₹3 lakh. The owner refused. Which limitation of controlling explains her decision?

options.text_md: Resistance from employees
Little control on external factors
Controlling is a primary function
Controlling is a costly affair

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Controlling is a costly affair. Control involves expense, time and effort; a small firm must check that the benefit is worth the cost. Here the system would cost more than a year's profit. "Primary function" describes planning and is not a limitation.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes the relationship between **planning** and **controlling**?

options.text_md: Controlling must be completed before planning begins
Planning and controlling are unrelated functions
Once a plan is made, controlling is not required
Planning without controlling is meaningless, and controlling without planning is blind

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Planning without controlling is meaningless, and controlling without planning is blind. Plans give the standards that controlling uses, and controlling tells whether plans are being achieved, so each depends on the other. The other statements deny this link or reverse the order.

questions.stem_md: Controlling findings at Tarang Paints (imagined) showed that the sales targets for the hills were unrealistic, so next year's plan set lower targets there. This shows that

options.text_md: controlling is only a backward-looking function
planning is a backward-looking function
controlling provides information that helps in better planning
controlling makes planning unnecessary

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** controlling provides information that helps in better planning. Information from control is fed back into the next plan, which shows the two functions are linked and that controlling looks forward too. Planning still remains necessary.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Controlling helps an organisation accomplish its goals.

**Reason (R):** Controlling measures progress towards goals and brings to light deviations so that corrective action can be taken.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: by spotting deviations early and correcting them, controlling keeps the organisation on course to its goals.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Controlling is a backward-looking as well as a forward-looking function.

**Reason (R):** Controlling is performed only after all activities of the year are over.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: controlling is a continuous function carried out throughout the year, not only at its end.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** It is difficult to control the job satisfaction of employees precisely.

**Reason (R):** Controlling cannot influence factors such as government policy and changes in technology.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. A is about the difficulty of measuring qualitative factors; R is about external factors, a different limitation.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A good control system helps in the efficient use of resources.

**Reason (R):** Under control, each activity is performed according to predetermined standards, which reduces waste and spoilage.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: working to standards means materials, money and time are not wasted.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Controlling is needed only in large business organisations, not in schools, hospitals or small shops.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Controlling is pervasive: every organisation, large or small, business or non-business, needs to check that work goes according to plan.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Controlling is a continuous process: setting standards, measuring, comparing and correcting go on throughout the life of an organisation.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Control is not a one-time check; managers keep reviewing performance against standards as work goes on.

questions.stem_md: Planning without controlling is meaningless, and controlling without planning is ___.
questions.solution_md: Controlling without planning is blind, because there would be no standards to check against.

questions.stem_md: Match each situation at the imagined Ganga Dairy cooperative with the importance of controlling it shows.

options.text_md: Milk spoilage fell after chilling temperatures were checked twice a day
Collection centres knew their daily targets, so drivers and chilling plants worked in step
A target that no centre could ever meet was lowered after review
Staff knew how their work would be appraised and worked harder

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Less spoilage means less waste of milk; balanced targets keep departments in step; reviewing an impossible target tests the standard; a clear basis of appraisal motivates staff.

questions.stem_md: State the meaning of controlling and give any two of its features.
questions.solution_md: One mark for the meaning, one for two correct features.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Controlling** is the function of seeing that **actual performance conforms to the plan** and correcting it where it does not.
**Features:** (1) it is **goal-oriented**; (2) it is **pervasive**, done by managers at all levels in every organisation. (Also: continuous; backward- and forward-looking.)

questions.stem_md: How are planning and controlling inseparable? Explain in two points.
questions.solution_md: Show the dependence in both directions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Planning gives the standards:** without a plan, control has nothing to measure against.
2. **Controlling checks the plan:** without control, managers cannot know whether the plan is working, and its findings help improve the next plan.

marking_scheme.step: Planning is the base of controlling

questions.stem_md: Explain any two limitations of controlling.
questions.solution_md: Any two limitations, each with a brief explanation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Difficulty in setting quantitative standards:** behaviour, morale and job satisfaction are hard to express in numbers, so control over them is weak.
2. **Costly affair:** control systems need money, time and effort; for a small firm the cost may be more than the benefit.

questions.stem_md: With an example of an imagined coaching institute, show how controlling is both backward-looking and forward-looking.
questions.solution_md: An example that looks at past results and then improves the future.

answer.model_answer_md: At an imagined coaching institute in Kota, the director compares last term's test results of each batch with the target (**backward-looking**). Finding one batch weak in physics, she plans extra classes and a new teacher for next term (**forward-looking**).

questions.stem_md: Explain any three points of importance of controlling for an organisation.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct points, each explained in a line.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Accomplishing goals:** it keeps measuring progress and corrects deviations, so the organisation stays on course.
2. **Efficient use of resources:** activities follow standards, which cuts waste and spoilage.
3. **Order and discipline:** close checks reduce dishonest behaviour among employees. (Also: judging accuracy of standards, motivation, coordination.)

questions.stem_md: Kiran runs a chain of 12 tea stalls in Pune (imagined). She wants to control the taste of tea, the friendliness of staff and the amount of milk used. Which of these will be easiest and which hardest to control? Give reasons and name the limitation involved.
questions.solution_md: Classify by measurability and name the limitation.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Easiest:** the **amount of milk**, because it can be measured in litres per day and compared with a standard.
**Hardest:** **friendliness of staff** (and, to some extent, taste), because they cannot be expressed in numbers.
**Limitation:** **difficulty in setting quantitative standards**, so control over such qualities depends on judgement and customer feedback.

questions.stem_md: A good control system is said to be the key to a well-run organisation. Explain any five points of importance of controlling.
questions.solution_md: Five distinct points, each with a heading and an explanation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Accomplishing organisational goals:** progress is measured and deviations are corrected in time.
2. **Judging accuracy of standards:** a careful review shows whether standards are too high or too low.
3. **Efficient use of resources:** working to standards reduces waste of material, money and time.
4. **Improving employee motivation:** people know what is expected and how they will be appraised.
5. **Ensuring order and discipline:** close checks curb dishonest behaviour. (Also: facilitating coordination, since every department works to balanced standards.)

questions.stem_md: "Controlling is necessary, but it cannot work miracles." Evaluate this statement by explaining the limitations of controlling and suggesting how a manager can reduce any one of them.
questions.solution_md: Four limitations and one practical remedy, with a conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Quantitative standards are hard** for morale, behaviour or job satisfaction, so control over them is imprecise.
2. **Little control on external factors** such as policy changes, technology or competition.
3. **Resistance from employees**, who may see close checks as a restriction on their freedom.
4. **Costly affair:** control needs money, time and effort, which a small firm may not afford.
5. **Reducing one:** resistance can be reduced by **involving employees** in setting standards and explaining the purpose of controls. So controlling helps greatly, but within limits.

questions.stem_md: Explain the relationship between planning and controlling. Is planning only forward-looking and controlling only backward-looking? Justify your answer.
questions.solution_md: Three points on the relationship and two on why the "one-way" view is wrong.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Planning is the base of controlling:** it sets the goals and standards against which performance is measured.
2. **Controlling makes plans effective:** it checks whether work goes as planned and corrects deviations.
3. **They are inseparable:** planning without controlling is meaningless; controlling without planning is blind.
4. **Planning also looks back:** plans are made using past experience and the results of earlier control.
5. **Controlling also looks forward:** its corrective action and revised standards improve future performance. So the two are **forward- and backward-looking** together.

questions.stem_md: The first step in the controlling process is

options.text_md: measurement of actual performance
setting performance standards
taking corrective action
analysing deviations

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** setting performance standards. Standards must exist before anything can be measured or compared, so setting them comes first. Measuring, analysing deviations and correcting follow in that order.

questions.stem_md: Which is the **last** step of the controlling process?

options.text_md: Taking corrective action
Comparing actual performance with standards
Setting performance standards
Measurement of actual performance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Taking corrective action. Control ends with action to remove the causes of deviation (or to revise the standard). The other steps come before it.

questions.stem_md: "Improve customer goodwill in the coming year" and "produce 2,000 helmets a day" are examples of standards that are respectively

options.text_md: quantitative and qualitative
qualitative and quantitative
both quantitative
both qualitative

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** qualitative and quantitative. Goodwill cannot be expressed in numbers, so it is a qualitative standard; 2,000 helmets a day is a number, so it is quantitative.

questions.stem_md: Why should performance standards be set in **precise and flexible** terms?

options.text_md: So that employees cannot understand them
So that they never need to be changed
So that only top managers can use them
So that performance can be measured against them and they can be revised when conditions change

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** So that performance can be measured against them and they can be revised when conditions change. Precise standards make measurement possible; flexibility allows changes when circumstances change. Standards must be understood by employees and are used at all levels.

questions.stem_md: A supervisor at Nirmal Soaps (imagined) picks 50 soap cakes from every batch and checks their weight. Which step of controlling, and which technique, is this?

options.text_md: Measurement of actual performance, by sample checking
Setting performance standards, by personal observation
Taking corrective action, by sample checking
Comparing performance, by a performance report

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Measurement of actual performance, by sample checking. Weighing some cakes measures what has actually been produced; checking a sample from each batch is the technique of sample checking. Standards are set earlier and correction comes later.

questions.stem_md: Unity Courier (imagined) aims to deliver 98 per cent of parcels within 48 hours. In June, it delivered 93 per cent. Noting this gap is the step of

options.text_md: setting performance standards
taking corrective action
comparing actual performance with standards
measurement of actual performance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** comparing actual performance with standards. Putting the actual figure (93) beside the standard (98) to find the gap is comparison. Setting the 98 per cent aim was the first step, measuring the 93 per cent was the second, and correction comes after analysis.

questions.stem_md: At Prakash Auto Parts (imagined), a 2 per cent rise in the cost of steel affects profit far more than a 20 per cent rise in the cost of stationery. Management therefore watches steel cost closely. This is the principle of

options.text_md: management by exception
unity of command
critical point control
scalar chain

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** critical point control. Critical point control means focusing on key result areas that affect the whole organisation; steel is such an area. Management by exception is about reporting only significant deviations; unity of command and scalar chain are Fayol principles.

questions.stem_md: The manager of Hira Garments (imagined) is informed only when daily output falls short of the target by more than 5 per cent; smaller gaps are handled by supervisors. This is

options.text_md: management by exception
critical point control
functional foremanship
decentralisation of control standards

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** management by exception. Only significant deviations beyond a permissible limit are brought to the manager's attention, which is management by exception. Critical point control is about which areas matter most, not about the size of the gap.

questions.stem_md: Which is a benefit of **management by exception**?

options.text_md: It ensures that every small deviation is reported to the managing director
It removes the need for setting standards
It makes corrective action unnecessary
It saves the time and effort of managers, who deal only with significant deviations

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It saves the time and effort of managers, who deal only with significant deviations. By filtering out minor deviations, managers can concentrate on important problems. Reporting everything is the opposite of the principle, and standards and correction are still needed.

questions.stem_md: Output at a printing press in Sivakasi (imagined) fell short because the machines were old. The **appropriate corrective action** is to

options.text_md: lower the output standard permanently without any review
repair or replace the machines
hire more salespeople
reduce the price of printed goods

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** repair or replace the machines. Corrective action must address the cause of deviation: here, defective machinery. Lowering the standard ignores the cause, and more salespeople or lower prices do not fix production.

questions.stem_md: Sales at Mitra Electronics (imagined) fell below target because a rival cut prices sharply. During **analysing deviations**, the manager should first

options.text_md: identify the cause of the deviation, which here lies outside the firm
punish the sales staff for the shortfall
stop measuring sales for the year
ignore the deviation, since it is not significant

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** identify the cause of the deviation, which here lies outside the firm. Analysis means finding why the deviation occurred; the cause here is external (competition), so blaming staff would be unfair. Measurement must continue, and a sharp fall in sales is significant.

questions.stem_md: If actual performance matches the standard or the deviation is within the permissible limit, the manager should

options.text_md: change the whole plan immediately
take no corrective action and let the work continue
replace the employees concerned
stop the measurement of performance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** take no corrective action and let the work continue. Control acts only on deviations beyond acceptable limits; otherwise work continues as planned. The other actions are unnecessary.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Under management by exception, minor deviations are not brought to the notice of top management.

**Reason (R):** Trying to control everything may end up in controlling nothing.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: if managers chase every small deviation, they have no time for important ones, so only significant deviations are reported.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Critical point control means that every activity of the organisation should be controlled with equal attention.

**Reason (R):** Key result areas are those that affect the working of the entire organisation.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: critical point control focuses attention on key result areas, not on every activity equally. R is true.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Setting performance standards is the first step of controlling.

**Reason (R):** Actual performance can be judged only against a predetermined criterion.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: without a standard there is nothing to compare actual performance with.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The performance of a hotel receptionist can be measured only in numbers, so customer feedback is useless for controlling.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Many standards, such as courtesy, are qualitative; customer feedback, observation and ratings are useful ways to measure them.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Sometimes the corrective action is to revise the standard itself, if analysis shows it was unrealistic.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** When deviations persist because the standard was set too high or too low, the right step is to revise it.

questions.stem_md: Focusing control on key result areas that affect the entire organisation is known as ___ ___ control.
questions.solution_md: This is critical point control.

questions.stem_md: Checking only a part of the output to judge the whole is the measurement technique called ___ checking.
questions.solution_md: It is sample checking: a few items are tested to judge a whole batch.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps of the controlling process followed at an imagined bicycle factory in Ludhiana in the correct order.

options.text_md: Compare the daily count with 300
Fix the target of 300 bicycles a day
Repair the faulty conveyor belt and retrain new workers
Find out why output fell short on some days
Count the bicycles actually assembled each day

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (e) → (a) → (d) → (c). Setting standards, measuring, comparing, analysing deviations and taking corrective action, in that order.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Match each action at the imagined Sona Rice Mill with the step of the controlling process it belongs to.

options.text_md: Deciding that broken grains must not exceed 3 per cent
Testing samples from each day's output for broken grains
Finding that the huller blades were worn out
Replacing the huller blades

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). A limit on broken grains is a standard; testing samples measures performance; finding worn blades is the cause behind the deviation; replacing them is correction.

questions.stem_md: An imagined shoe unit in Agra has a standard output of 500 pairs a day. On Monday it produced 460 pairs. Calculate the deviation as a percentage of the standard.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Deviation = 500 − 460 = 40 pairs.
Step 2: Percentage deviation = 40 ÷ 500 × 100 = 8. So the deviation is 8% of the standard.

questions.stem_md: An imagined pickle maker in Guntur set a standard cost of ₹200 per jar. The actual cost last month was ₹212 per jar. By what percentage did the actual cost exceed the standard?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Deviation = 212 − 200 = ₹12 per jar.
Step 2: 12 ÷ 200 × 100 = 6. So the cost exceeded the standard by 6%.

questions.stem_md: The electricity budget of an imagined cold-storage firm in Agra is ₹80,000 a month; last month it spent ₹86,000. Under management by exception, only deviations above 5% are reported to the general manager. Find the percentage deviation (the report decision follows from it).
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Deviation = 86,000 − 80,000 = ₹6,000.
Step 2: 6,000 ÷ 80,000 × 100 = 7.5.
Step 3: 7.5% is more than the 5% limit, so it must be reported to the general manager.

questions.stem_md: A furniture workshop in Saharanpur (imagined) allowed 1,200 labour hours for an order but used 1,320 hours. Calculate the excess hours as a percentage of the standard.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Excess = 1,320 − 1,200 = 120 hours.
Step 2: 120 ÷ 1,200 × 100 = 10. So the excess is 10%.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between critical point control and management by exception.
questions.solution_md: One is about the areas to control, the other about the size of deviations to report.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Critical point control** decides **which areas** to watch: the key result areas, such as raw-material cost or safety, that affect the whole organisation.
**Management by exception** decides **which deviations** reach senior managers: only those beyond a permissible limit.

questions.stem_md: Explain the second step of the controlling process and name two techniques used in it.
questions.solution_md: Name and explain the step, then two techniques.

answer.model_answer_md:
The second step is **measurement of actual performance**: performance is measured in the same units as the standard, objectively and reliably.
**Techniques:** personal observation, sample checking, performance reports.

questions.stem_md: Suggest a corrective action for each deviation at an imagined toy factory in Channapatna: (i) many toys fail quality checks because workers are new; (ii) output is low because the paint supply arrives late.
questions.solution_md: Each action must remove the cause given.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Arrange **training** for the new workers, with closer supervision for a few weeks.
(ii) Improve **purchasing**: place orders earlier, keep a buffer stock of paint or add a second supplier.

questions.stem_md: Explain the first three steps of the controlling process.
questions.solution_md: Three steps in order, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Setting performance standards:** targets in quantitative (units, cost, time) or qualitative (goodwill, morale) terms, precise and flexible.
2. **Measuring actual performance** in the same units as the standards, by observation, sample checking or reports.
3. **Comparing actual with standards** to find out whether, and by how much, performance deviates.

questions.stem_md: Why is it not enough to find that a deviation exists? Explain what a manager does while analysing deviations.
questions.solution_md: Reason for analysis, the two principles, and identification of cause.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A deviation shows only **that** something went wrong, not **why**; correction without the cause may fail.
2. The manager uses **critical point control** to check whether the deviation is in a **key result area**, and **management by exception** to judge whether it is **beyond the permissible limit**.
3. The manager then finds the **cause**, such as faulty machines, untrained workers, unrealistic standards or outside factors.

questions.stem_md: The production manager of an imagined fan maker allows a deviation of up to 5%. Electricity cost was budgeted at ₹80,000 and the actual cost was ₹86,000. Calculate the percentage deviation, state whether it should be reported, and name the principle used.
questions.solution_md: Compute the percentage, compare with the limit, name the principle.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Deviation:** the actual cost was ₹86,000 against a budget of ₹80,000, an excess of ₹6,000. As a share of the standard this is 6,000 ÷ 80,000 × 100 = **7.5%**.
**Decision:** 7.5% is more than the permissible 5%, so the deviation is significant and **should be reported** to the production manager, who must find its cause and take corrective action.
**Principle:** this is **management by exception**: smaller gaps within the limit are left to supervisors, so that the manager can concentrate on the deviations that really matter.

questions.stem_md: Explain the five steps of the controlling process.
questions.solution_md: Five steps in order, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Setting performance standards:** quantitative or qualitative targets, precise and flexible.
2. **Measurement of actual performance:** in the same units as the standards, through observation, sample checks or reports.
3. **Comparing actual performance with standards:** reveals the size of the deviation.
4. **Analysing deviations:** using critical point control (key result areas) and management by exception (beyond permissible limits), and finding the cause.
5. **Taking corrective action:** remove the cause, e.g. repair machines, retrain workers, or revise unrealistic standards; no action if within limits.

questions.stem_md: A newly appointed manager of an imagined supermarket chain wants to check every item, every bill and every employee personally. Using the ideas of critical point control and management by exception, advise her on a better approach.
questions.solution_md: Diagnose the problem, apply both principles to the case, and show the benefits.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Problem:** checking everything wastes her time; "trying to control everything may end in controlling nothing".
2. **Critical point control:** identify **key result areas**, such as stock losses, cash collection and fresh-food wastage, and watch them closely.
3. **Management by exception:** fix **permissible limits**, e.g. stock loss up to 1 per cent, and ask supervisors to report only deviations beyond them.
4. **Benefits:** saves her time, lets her focus on serious problems and speeds up action.
5. **Delegation:** supervisors handle minor deviations, which also develops them.

questions.stem_md: Corrective action depends on the cause of the deviation. Suggest a corrective action for each of five causes of deviation in an imagined garment export unit in Tiruppur.
questions.solution_md: Five causes, each with a matching corrective action.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Defective machinery:** sewing machines that break down often should be repaired or replaced, with a schedule of preventive maintenance.
2. **Untrained workers:** new tailors who make stitching errors need training and closer supervision for some weeks.
3. **Shortage of raw material:** late fabric supply can be prevented by ordering earlier, keeping a buffer stock and adding a second supplier.
4. **Low morale:** absenteeism and slow work call for better incentives, recognition and prompt handling of grievances.
5. **Unrealistic standards:** if no line can ever meet the target, the standard itself should be revised after a careful review.
